content: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted virus in the United States. There are approximately 40 types of HPV, and each year, an additional 2 million people become infected. HPV is transmitted through sexual contact. Most HPV infections do not cause symptoms and resolve on their own. However, HPV is significant because it can lead to cervical cancer in women. Each year, about 10,000 women are diagnosed with cervical cancer, and 3,700 die from it. Globally, it is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths among women. HPV is also linked to other, less common cancers in both men and women. Additionally, it can cause genital warts and warts in the upper respiratory tract. Over 50% of sexually active men and women will be infected with HPV at some point in their lives. While there is no treatment for the HPV infection itself, the conditions it causes can be treated. The HPV vaccine is an inactivated (non-live) vaccine that protects against four major types of HPV. Two of these types are responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancer cases, and the other two cause about 90% of genital warts. The vaccine can prevent most cases of genital warts and cervical cancer. Protection from the vaccine is expected to be long-lasting. However, vaccinated women still need regular cervical cancer screenings because the vaccine does not protect against all HPV types that can cause cervical cancer. The HPV vaccine is routinely recommended for girls aged 11–12 years, though it can be administered to girls as young as 9 years old. It is crucial for girls to receive the vaccine before their first sexual contact, as they are unlikely to have been exposed to HPV at that point. For these individuals, the vaccine can prevent nearly 100% of diseases caused by the four targeted HPV types. However, if a girl or woman is already infected with a specific HPV type, the vaccine will not prevent disease caused by that type. The vaccine is also recommended for girls and women aged 13–26 who did not receive it earlier. The vaccine is administered in a three-dose series: the first dose is given immediately, the second dose two months later, and the third dose six months after the first. Additional booster doses are not recommended. The HPV vaccine can be given alongside other vaccines. Certain individuals should not receive the HPV vaccine or should delay vaccination. These include anyone who has had a life-threatening allergic reaction to yeast, any component of the HPV vaccine, or a previous dose of the vaccine. Pregnant women should not receive the vaccine, although it appears to be safe for both the mother and the unborn baby. Research is ongoing. Receiving the vaccine during pregnancy is not a reason to consider terminating the pregnancy. Breastfeeding women can safely receive the vaccine. Women who discover they were pregnant when they received the vaccine are encouraged to contact the HPV vaccine in pregnancy registry at 800-986-8999. This registry collects information to help understand how pregnant women respond to the vaccine. People with mild illnesses can still receive the vaccine, but those with moderate or severe illnesses should wait until they recover. The HPV vaccine does not appear to cause serious side effects. However, like any medicine, it could potentially cause severe problems, such as a serious allergic reaction. The risk of a vaccine causing severe harm or death is extremely small. Mild problems associated with the vaccine include pain at the injection site (experienced by about 8 in 10 people), redness or swelling at the injection site (about 1 in 4), mild fever (100°F, about 1 in 10), itching at the injection site (about 1 in 30), and moderate fever (102°F, about 1 in 65). These symptoms are short-lived and resolve on their own. Life-threatening allergic reactions to vaccines are very rare. If they occur, they typically happen within minutes to a few hours after vaccination. Like all vaccines, the HPV vaccine will continue to be monitored for unusual or severe problems. If a severe reaction occurs, you should look for unusual conditions such as a high fever or behavior changes. Signs of a serious allergic reaction include difficulty breathing, hoarseness or wheezing, hives, paleness, weakness, a rapid heartbeat, or dizziness. If any of these occur, contact a doctor or seek medical attention immediately. Inform the doctor about what happened, the date and time it occurred, and when the vaccination was given. You can also ask your healthcare provider to file a Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) form, or you can file one yourself by calling 1-800-822-7967 or visiting the VAERS website. In the rare event of a serious reaction to a vaccine, the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) is available to help cover the costs of care for those who have been harmed. For more information about the VICP, call 1-800-338-2382 or visit their website. For additional information, consult your doctor or healthcare provider. They can provide the vaccine package insert or suggest other sources of information. You can also contact your local or state health department’s immunization program or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) by calling 1-800-232-4636 (1-800-CDC-INFO) or visiting the National Immunization Program’s website.
